_meta.purpose: Researched fun facts for recipes ALREADY on arecipe.bsky.social. Prep only — NOT published; the funFact lexicon field does not exist yet (pending the recipe-model design pass). Apply via a Phase-9-style putRecord op once the field lands.
_meta.factCheck: Verified 2026-07-09: sloppy joe, cobb salad, refried-beans mistranslation, barbacoa->barbecue, buffalo wings 1964, chicken tikka masala (UK), butter chicken (Moti Mahal), moussaka (Tselementes 1920s), carbonara (post-WWII Rome). Others from established culinary history; "Legend says" used only where grounded and not contradicted.

funFacts.name: Banana Bread
funFacts.funFact: Banana bread took off in 1930s Depression kitchens — thrift plus the new mass-market baking soda made mashing up overripe bananas irresistible.

funFacts.name: Sloppy Joes
funFacts.funFact: Commonly credited to a cook named Joe in Sioux City, Iowa in the 1930s, who added tomato sauce to a loose-meat sandwich (a Havana bar owner also claims a version).

funFacts.name: Coleslaw
funFacts.funFact: The name comes straight from the Dutch 'koolsla' — 'kool' (cabbage) + 'sla' (salad).

funFacts.name: Chili con Carne
funFacts.funFact: Chili is the official state dish of Texas, and a traditional Texas 'bowl of red' contains no beans at all.

funFacts.name: Caesar Salad
funFacts.funFact: Invented in Tijuana, Mexico in 1924 by Italian immigrant Caesar Cardini — not in Italy, and nothing to do with Julius Caesar.

funFacts.name: Cobb Salad
funFacts.funFact: Legend says restaurateur Robert Cobb threw it together from Brown Derby fridge leftovers late one night in 1930s Hollywood.

funFacts.name: Southern Fried Chicken
funFacts.funFact: It blends two traditions: Scottish deep-frying and the seasoning and technique of West African cooks in the American South.

funFacts.name: BBQ Pulled Pork
funFacts.funFact: 'Barbecue' itself comes from the Taino word 'barbacoa' — a wooden frame for slow-cooking meat over smoke, seen by Spanish explorers in the Caribbean.

funFacts.name: Mac and Cheese
funFacts.funFact: Thomas Jefferson helped popularize mac and cheese in America, serving it at an 1802 White House dinner after falling for pasta in Europe.

funFacts.name: Chilaquiles Rojos
funFacts.funFact: The name is Nahuatl (Aztec) for roughly 'chilis and greens' — and it's a thrifty way to use up day-old tortillas.

funFacts.name: Huevos Rancheros
funFacts.funFact: The name means 'rancher's eggs' — a hearty mid-morning breakfast served on rural Mexican farms.

funFacts.name: Salsa Verde
funFacts.funFact: It's built on the tomatillo, a husk-wrapped fruit the Aztecs cultivated long before the red tomato dominated Mexican kitchens.

funFacts.name: Birria Tacos
funFacts.funFact: Birria is a celebration stew from Jalisco, traditionally made with goat; the viral crispy 'quesabirria' taco is a much newer U.S. spin.

funFacts.name: Ground Beef Tacos
funFacts.funFact: The crunchy hard-shell taco is largely a U.S. creation — popularized by Glen Bell (Taco Bell) in the 1950s, apart from Mexico's soft corn tortillas.

funFacts.name: Chicken Fajitas
funFacts.funFact: 'Fajita' comes from the Spanish 'faja' (strip/belt), for the skirt steak Texas ranch hands originally grilled.

funFacts.name: Mexican Rice
funFacts.funFact: In Mexico this tomato-tinted rice is called 'sopa seca' — a 'dry soup' course served before the main dish.

funFacts.name: Refried Beans
funFacts.funFact: 'Refried' is a mistranslation: 'frijoles refritos' means 'well-fried,' not fried twice — the Spanish 're-' here is emphasis.

funFacts.name: Elote
funFacts.funFact: Grilled Mexican street corn celebrates maize, which was domesticated in Mexico roughly 9,000 years ago.

funFacts.name: Pork Tamales
funFacts.funFact: Tamales are pre-Columbian fast food: corn-husk-wrapped parcels the Aztecs and Maya carried to work and made communally for feasts.

funFacts.name: Pozole Rojo
funFacts.funFact: Pozole is built on hominy — corn treated with lime (nixtamalization) — and was a ceremonial dish in Aztec times.

funFacts.name: Chicken Enchiladas
funFacts.funFact: Wrapping food in tortillas is ancient Mesoamerican practice: people in the Valley of Mexico ate small fish rolled in tortillas long before Spanish contact.

funFacts.name: Cheese Enchiladas
funFacts.funFact: 'Enchilada' simply means 'seasoned with chili' — the dish traces back to the corn-tortilla wraps of the Maya and Aztecs.

funFacts.name: Beef Barbacoa
funFacts.funFact: The word 'barbecue' descends from 'barbacoa,' a Taino term for the wooden frame used to slow-cook meat over smoke.

funFacts.name: Carnitas
funFacts.funFact: Carnitas ('little meats') come from Michoacan, where pork is gently confit-cooked in its own fat until tender then crisped.

funFacts.name: Pico de Gallo
funFacts.funFact: Its name means 'rooster's beak' in Spanish — nobody's certain why, though eating it pinched between fingers is one theory.

funFacts.name: Guacamole
funFacts.funFact: The name is Nahuatl: 'ahuacamolli' — 'avocado sauce' — a dish the Aztecs were making centuries ago.

funFacts.name: Apple Pie
funFacts.funFact: Apple pie isn't American in origin: the earliest recorded recipe is English, c. 1381, with no sugar and a hard 'coffin' crust meant as a baking vessel.

funFacts.name: Classic Meatloaf
funFacts.funFact: Minced-meat loaves date back to Roman cookbooks; the American meatloaf surged during the Depression as a way to stretch a little meat.

funFacts.name: Crispy Baked Buffalo Wings
funFacts.funFact: Buffalo wings were invented in 1964 at the Anchor Bar in Buffalo, New York, when Teressa Bellissimo fried up wings as a late-night snack.

funFacts.name: Tacos al Pastor
funFacts.funFact: 'Al pastor' means 'shepherd style' — the spit-roasted pork technique came from Lebanese immigrants' shawarma, adapted with Mexican chilis.

funFacts.name: Mango Sticky Rice
funFacts.funFact: Thailand's beloved 'khao niao mamuang' peaks in the hot season, when mangoes are ripe and paired with coconut-soaked glutinous rice.

funFacts.name: Chicken Biryani
funFacts.funFact: Biryani descends from Mughal-era layered rice dishes, finished with the sealed-pot 'dum' method that steams meat and rice together.

funFacts.name: Chicken Tikka Masala
funFacts.funFact: Widely believed to have been invented in Britain (Glasgow, 1970s); in 2001 a UK foreign secretary called it 'a true British national dish.'

funFacts.name: Butter Chicken
funFacts.funFact: Born at Delhi's Moti Mahal in the 1950s, when cooks simmered leftover tandoori chicken in a buttery tomato gravy to keep it from drying out.

funFacts.name: Coq au Vin
funFacts.funFact: The dish was designed to tenderize a tough old rooster ('coq') by long, slow braising in acidic red wine.

funFacts.name: Beef Bourguignon
funFacts.funFact: A rustic Burgundy peasant stew for tenderizing tough beef, later elevated to haute cuisine by chef Auguste Escoffier.

funFacts.name: Greek Chicken Souvlaki with Tzatziki
funFacts.funFact: 'Souvlaki' means 'little skewer' — Greeks have grilled meat on skewers since antiquity (charred skewer sets survive from the Bronze Age).

funFacts.name: Moussaka
funFacts.funFact: The béchamel-topped moussaka Greeks know today was created in the 1920s by French-trained chef Nikolaos Tselementes.

funFacts.name: Spaghetti Carbonara
funFacts.funFact: Carbonara's origin is fiercely debated; the best-supported theory ties it to 1944 Rome, marrying local pasta with American ration bacon and eggs.

funFacts.name: Pad Thai
funFacts.funFact: Pad Thai was promoted by the Thai government in the 1930s-40s to build national identity and cut rice consumption during hard times.

funFacts.name: Greek Cucumber Tomato Feta Salad
funFacts.funFact: 'Horiatiki' means 'village salad' — authentically it has no lettuce and is crowned with a whole slab of feta.
